html:
A bazaar district in the old centre of Cairo, named after a caravanserai built around 1382 by the emir Jaharkas al-Khalili, an officer of the Mamluk sultan Barquq.

A khan, or caravanserai, was a building where merchants lodged and stored their goods, with stables and storerooms round a courtyard. Al-Khalili built his on ground that had belonged to the palaces of the Fatimid caliphs. In the early 1500s Sultan al-Ghuri rebuilt the area with new shops and gates, some of which still stand.

Under the Mamluk Sultanate Cairo sat on the spice route between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean, and the khan quarter was one of its main markets for foreign merchants. Later it became the heart of a maze of streets selling metalwork, spices, cloth and jewellery.

It lies beside al-Azhar and the shrine of al-Husayn. Naguib Mahfouz named a novel after it in 1945. Today it is busy with both tourists and Cairenes.
sum: A bazaar district in the old centre of Cairo, named after a caravanserai built around 1382 by the emir Jaharkas al-Khalili, an officer of the Mamluk sultan Barquq.
